To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified a new PCD-causing gene and that we have identified the first human gene that is required for the proper assembly of both radial spokes and the central complex in cilia.
we identified mutations in the gene RSPH3 as a cause of Primary Ciliary Dyskin...
we identified RSPH3 as a novel PCD gene and we demonstrated that RSPH23 and RSPH3 are essential for the proper formation of RSs and CC in human airway epithelial cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genetic causes of PCD and with the understanding of the pathophysiology of the condition.
the identification of genes involved in the pathophysiology of PCD and the development of new diagnostic methods for this rare condition.
the identification of new PCD genes and the characterization of the associated phenotype.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RSPH1, RSPH3 and RSPH6 (the three RSPH genes) are the three main genes encoding RS-head proteins in humans.
mutations in RSPH3 cause PCD with a CC/RS phenotype.
RSPH1, RSPH3 and RSPH9 are the only genes known to be involved in PCD due to RS defects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mutations in the gene RSPH3 cause primary ciliary dysknesia in a significant fraction of patients with ciliopathies.
mutations in RSPH3 cause PCD with a near absence of detectible RSs and CC defects in cilia and spermatozoa.
the RSPH3 mutation is associated with PCD, and that RSPH23 and RSPH3 are the only proteins in RSs that are not associated with PCD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RSPH23, RSPH1, RSPH4, and RSPH3 are all required for the assembly of RSs in humans.
RSPH23 and RSPH3 should be considered as candidate genes for the diagnosis of PCD-CC/RS defects.
CC/RS defects can be caused by a wide spectrum of mutations, including those that affect RS proteins.
